items.title: Menopause symptoms aren’t always taken seriously. These female lawmakers plan to change that
items.standfirst: From Utah to Louisiana, US states are making menopause care more affordable and accessible for midlife womenMelissa Shusterman was desperate for help with her menopausal symptoms: body aches, lethargy and brain fog, which she described as feeling “not myself”. The Pennsylvania state representative saw a gynecologist, a physical therapist, a chiropractor and a urologist. One doctor gave her lubricant, even though she’d already explained to him that sex was not the problem. (“Have you seen my husband?” she quipped.)“I am more than lubrication,” Shusterman said. “I am a dynamic, smart, hardworking woman who wants to continue to feel good, so I can join my contemporaries, get back to work, and change things.” Continue reading...

clusters.title: Damaging the lifeline that Samaritans offers the public | Letters
clusters.neutral_headline: Damaging the lifeline that Samaritans offers the public | Letters

items.title: Damaging the lifeline that Samaritans offers the public | Letters
items.standfirst: Volunteers despair as the charity sets about closing local branches and restructuringSamaritans old and new will, I’m sure, have been just as shocked as I was by your article (‘Is anyone up for a fight?’: The battle for the soul of Samaritans, 10 November). Many, though, will not be surprised. I was a volunteer for 26 years in three branches. The work was demanding and life-changing; the experience is so transformative that it gives every part of society people who are strong enough to bear others’ burdens and able to share their pain. We don’t stop being listeners when we stop being volunteers.During my time, I found that the people at the top were detached from what went on at branch level. It is not news to me that they cannot understand how central to the work each local branch is and how important every human contact is to those who need to talk. Continue reading...
